messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajan is a 58-year-old South Asian man who has spent the better part of three decades as a bomb disposal technician — a career built on the premise that composure under extreme pressure is not merely a professional asset but a moral identity. He is married, the father of two adult children, and by most external measures a man of formidable competence. He presented for psychological assessment with a PCL-5 score of 39, describing symptoms that had persisted for nearly two years following his younger son Arjun's sudden diagnosis of acute bacterial meningitis at age nineteen.

The event itself unfolded with a speed that Rajan still cannot reconcile. Arjun had complained of a headache on a Tuesday evening; by Wednesday morning he was unconscious in the ICU. Rajan remembers the corridor of the hospital with terrible precision — the antiseptic smell that hit him as the automatic doors opened, the sight of a nurse drawing up medication through a drip line at the nurses' station, the particular quality of fluorescent light on linoleum. For seventy-two hours, the outcome was genuinely uncertain. Arjun survived, but the weeks that followed — the IV lines, the monitoring equipment, the repeated blood draws — etched themselves into Rajan with a depth he did not anticipate and could not explain.

In the months after Arjun's discharge, Rajan began to notice that certain sensory details would pull him back without transition or warning. The smell of antiseptic cleaning solution — present in his workplace during routine equipment sterilisation — could instantly reconstitute the full scene: the ICU bay, the sound of monitors, Arjun's stillness beneath tubes and lines. These intrusions arrived with complete sensory immediacy, as though no time had passed, and the visual images — Arjun's face, the needles, the drip stand — were what surfaced most forcefully. What made this particularly destabilising was not merely the content of the memories but their involuntary, ambush-like quality; something in his surroundings could trigger the full reliving before he had any chance to orient himself. When the memories broke through in this way, his body responded with a force that alarmed him — heart hammering, hands cold, breath constricted — as though the threat were present and immediate rather than two years past. The physical reactivity, arriving without consent, fed directly into a vigilance that now extended into the night; he lay awake telling himself he needed to stay alert, that something could shift without warning, that sleep was a form of dangerous inattention.

The negative appraisals that developed around these experiences became, in time, as disabling as the symptoms themselves. Rajan had come to believe, with quiet but absolute conviction, that what he was experiencing meant he was weak — that a man who had neutralised explosive devices in confined spaces for thirty years had no legitimate claim to be undone by a hospital visit. This belief did not stay contained. When a memory surfaced and his body reacted, the shame of the reaction compounded the distress, amplifying the threat and making the emotional state harder to regulate. He was also increasingly certain that the sheer uncontrollability of the intrusions — the way they arrived without invitation and felt entirely real — meant he was losing his mind. This fear of going crazy was not abstract; it was a daily interpretive lens through which each intrusive image confirmed further deterioration. The helplessness he felt — the recognition that he had been unable to protect his son, that he could not stop bad things from happening — circled back into the triggers themselves, so that being around children, including his own grandchildren, now carried a weight of anticipated catastrophe that made ordinary family gatherings feel dangerous. He had begun declining visits, offering work commitments as explanation.

At work, the sterilisation procedures for his team's equipment meant that the antiseptic smell was inescapable on certain shifts. He had not told his supervisor. The threat state these exposures generated — the physical reactivity, the negative emotions cycling through fear and guilt — reinforced his conviction that he was fundamentally changed and diminished. It was his wife who finally named what she was watching and told him, plainly, that she was frightened for him. What brought Rajan to the clinic was not that he agreed with her assessment, but that he could no longer argue against it. What he fears most is that he is right about himself. What he hopes, though he would not phrase it this way, is that he is wrong.
